summary.text: Writing \(m=\lfloor rn\rfloor\) and \(\alpha=rn-m\), irrationality gives \(0<\alpha<1\), while \(r^2=2r+\tfrac14\) reduces the error to \(2\alpha+(n/4-K)\), where \(K=\lfloor n/4+(2-r)\alpha\rfloor\). Since \(-\tfrac14<(2-r)\alpha<0\), splitting on \(n\bmod4\) shows \(\tfrac14\le n/4-K\le1\), and these bounds with \(0<\alpha<1\) give the two strict inequalities.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
r=\frac{2+\sqrt5}{2}=1+\frac{\sqrt5}{2},
\qquad
a(n)=\left\lfloor r\left\lfloor rn\right\rfloor\right\rfloor.
\]
We prove that for every integer \(n\ge 1\),
\[
\frac14<nr^2-a(n)<3.
\]
All floors below are ordinary integer floors.

First record two elementary facts about \(r\). Since
\[
2<\sqrt5<\frac52,
\]
we have
\[
2<r<\frac94.
\]
(The inequalities for \(\sqrt5\) follow by squaring the positive quantities involved: \(2^2<5<(5/2)^2\).) Also,
\[
r^2=\left(1+\frac{\sqrt5}{2}\right)^2
=1+\sqrt5+\frac54
=\frac94+\sqrt5,
\]
whereas
\[
2r+\frac14=2+\sqrt5+\frac14=\frac94+\sqrt5.
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{r^2=2r+\frac14}. \tag{1}
\]

Fix an integer \(n\ge1\), and put
\[
m=\lfloor rn\rfloor,
\qquad
\alpha=rn-m.
\]
Thus \(\alpha\) is the fractional part of \(rn\), so initially \(0\le\alpha<1\). In fact,
\[
\boxed{0<\alpha<1}. \tag{2}
\]
To see the strict lower bound, recall first that \(\sqrt5\) is irrational. Indeed, if \(\sqrt5=u/v\) for relatively prime positive integers \(u,v\), then \(u^2=5v^2\). Hence \(5\mid u^2\), so \(5\mid u\); writing \(u=5w\) then gives \(v^2=5w^2\), so \(5\mid v\), contradicting coprimality. Consequently \(r=1+\sqrt5/2\) is irrational. Since \(n\ne0\), the number \(rn\) is also irrational: if \(rn\) were rational, then dividing it by the nonzero integer \(n\) would make \(r\) rational. Therefore \(rn\) is not an integer, and its fractional part \(\alpha\) cannot be zero. This proves (2).

Because \(r>2\) and \(n\ge1\), we have \(rn>2\), and hence
\[
m=\lfloor rn\rfloor\ge2.
\]
In particular \(rm>0\), so its floor is nonnegative. Thus the nested floor defining \(a(n)\) is simply the nonnegative integer
\[
a(n)=\lfloor rm\rfloor. \tag{3}
\]

We next rewrite \(rm\) in a form whose integer part is easy to separate. From \(rn=m+\alpha\), or equivalently \(m=rn-\alpha\), and identity (1), we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
rm
&=r(rn-\alpha)\\
&=nr^2-r\alpha\\
&=n\left(2r+\frac14\right)-r\alpha\\
&=2rn+\frac n4-r\alpha\\
&=2(m+\alpha)+\frac n4-r\alpha\\
&=2m+\frac n4+(2-r)\alpha.
\end{aligned} \tag{4}
\]
Define
\[
K=\left\lfloor\frac n4+(2-r)\alpha\right\rfloor.
\]
Since \(2m\) is an integer, (4) and the rule \(\lfloor j+x\rfloor=j+\lfloor x\rfloor\) for integral \(j\) give
\[
a(n)=\lfloor rm\rfloor=2m+K. \tag{5}
\]

Now use (1), \(rn=m+\alpha\), and (5) to calculate the desired discrepancy:
\[
\begin{aligned}
nr^2-a(n)
&=n\left(2r+\frac14\right)-(2m+K)\\
&=2rn+\frac n4-2m-K\\
&=2(m+\alpha)+\frac n4-2m-K\\
&=2\alpha+\left(\frac n4-K\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{nr^2-a(n)=2\alpha+\left(\frac n4-K\right)}. \tag{6}
\]
It remains to control the correction \(n/4-K\).

For this purpose, set
\[
c=(2-r)\alpha.
\]
The bounds on \(r\) and \(\alpha\) imply
\[
\boxed{-\frac14<c<0}. \tag{7}
\]
Indeed, \(2<r<9/4\) says
\[
0<r-2<\frac14.
\]
Since \(0<\alpha<1\), multiplication gives
\[
0<(r-2)\alpha<\frac14,
\]
and negating yields (7).

Write the Euclidean division of \(n\) by \(4\) as
\[
n=4q+s,
\qquad q\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0},
\qquad s\in\{0,1,2,3\}.
\]
Then
\[
\frac n4=q+\frac s4,
\]
and hence
\[
K=\left\lfloor q+\frac s4+c\right\rfloor
=q+\left\lfloor\frac s4+c\right\rfloor. \tag{8}
\]
We now evaluate the final floor, splitting according to the residue \(s=n\bmod4\).

If \(s=0\), then by (7)
\[
-1< -\frac14<c<0.
\]
Therefore \(\lfloor c\rfloor=-1\). Equation (8) gives \(K=q-1\), and consequently
\[
\frac n4-K=q-(q-1)=1. \tag{9}
\]

If \(s\in\{1,2,3\}\), then \(s/4\ge1/4\). Since \(c>-1/4\),
\[
\frac s4+c>0.
\]
Also \(c<0\) and \(s/4\le3/4\), so
\[
\frac s4+c<\frac s4\le\frac34<1.
\]
Thus
\[
0<\frac s4+c<1,
\]
which implies
\[
\left\lfloor\frac s4+c\right\rfloor=0.
\]
Equation (8) therefore gives \(K=q\), and hence
\[
\frac n4-K=q+\frac s4-q=\frac s4. \tag{10}
\]

Equations (9) and (10) show explicitly that
\[
\frac n4-K=
\begin{cases}
1,&n\equiv0\pmod4,\\
\frac14,&n\equiv1\pmod4,\\
\frac12,&n\equiv2\pmod4,\\
\frac34,&n\equiv3\pmod4.
\end{cases}
\]
In particular,
\[
\boxed{\frac14\le\frac n4-K\le1}. \tag{11}
\]

Finally combine (2), (6), and (11). Since \(\alpha>0\),
\[
nr^2-a(n)
=2\alpha+\left(\frac n4-K\right)
>0+\frac14
=\frac14.
\]
Since \(\alpha<1\), we have \(2\alpha<2\), and therefore
\[
nr^2-a(n)
=2\alpha+\left(\frac n4-K\right)
<2+1
=3.
\]
Thus, for every integer \(n\ge1\),
\[
\boxed{\frac14<nr^2-a(n)<3},
\]
as required.
